client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away two months ago — it was so sudden, and I still can't believe he's gone. Everything feels kind of gray and flat, like nothing I used to enjoy even registers anymore. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: What you're carrying right now — the shock of losing your dad so suddenly, the numbness, the grayness — that's an enormous weight, and the quiet, almost exhausted way you're sharing this tells me just how deeply you're feeling it. It makes complete sense that you'd question whether talking can even help, because when grief flattens everything, hope itself can feel out of reach. The fact that you showed up and tried anyway, even through that doubt, is actually a meaningful and courageous first step.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not sure "courageous" is the right word — it feels more like desperation, honestly. Like I've just run out of other options and I don't know what else to do with myself. I guess I'm just worried that we'll talk and talk and at the end of it my dad will still be gone and I'll still feel this hollow.
therapist: There's something really honest and raw in what you just said — and I notice even as you describe feeling hollow and desperate, there's an urgency in how you're expressing it, like part of you is still fighting to find a way through this. You're absolutely right that talking won't bring your dad back, and I'd never want to pretend otherwise — grief isn't a problem to be solved, but the hollowness you're describing, that numbness that's taken over your life, that *can* shift. The goal isn't to make his absence hurt less, but to help you find a way to carry it without it swallowing you whole.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: That phrase "carry it without it swallowing you whole" actually got to me a little, because that's exactly what it feels like right now — like I'm being swallowed. But I don't even know what "carrying it" is supposed to look like in practice, like what does that actually mean day to day when you wake up and the first thought you have is that he's gone. I guess I'm asking because it sounds nice as a concept but I can't picture what it would feel like from where I'm standing.
therapist: The way you're asking that — quickly, softly, like you're reaching for something just out of grasp — tells me this isn't just a philosophical question, it's an urgent and very real one, and you deserve a real answer rather than more comforting abstractions. "Carrying it" in practice might look as small as getting through that first waking moment by letting the thought be there without immediately fighting it or collapsing into it — just noticing it, like a wave, and staying on your feet anyway. We can actually work on that together, building tiny, concrete moments of ground to stand on, rather than trying to leap to a place you can't yet picture from where you are right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The "wave" thing makes some sense to me, but I'm honestly not sure I know how to just "notice" something without either pushing it away or getting completely pulled under by it — those seem like the only two settings I have right now. Like this morning I woke up and thought about him and within about thirty seconds I was just lying there unable to move for almost an hour. I don't know if that's me collapsing into it or just... what grief is supposed to look like.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, pitched high, like your mind is racing even as you describe being unable to move — tells me that hour this morning is still very much with you right now, and I want you to know that what you experienced wasn't failure or "collapsing wrong," it was your whole system overwhelmed by an unbearable loss. Those two settings you described, pushing away or being pulled under, are actually a completely understandable response to pain this big — your mind hasn't yet learned there's a middle ground because it's never had to survive something like this before. That middle ground is real, and it's something we can gently practice together, not as a way of controlling grief, but of building just enough steadiness that the wave doesn't have to take the whole hour every time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's a little relieving to hear it wasn't me doing grief "wrong," because I've honestly been adding a layer of guilt on top of everything — like I should be functioning better by now, two months in. But when you say "practice," I get a little nervous, because in my experience when people say that they mean some kind of exercise or technique, and I'm not sure I trust myself to actually do it consistently when I can barely get out of bed some mornings. What would that even look like on a day when just existing feels like too much?
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but quick, like you're bracing for disappointment even as you're opening up a little — tells me that small lift of relief is fragile, and I want to be careful with it. I also want to gently challenge that guilt, because two months is not a deadline, and there is no "should be functioning better by now" — you lost your dad suddenly, and your nervous system is doing exactly what overwhelmed nervous systems do. And on the days when just existing is too much, "practice" might look like nothing more than placing one hand on your chest when the wave hits and taking a single breath — not to fix anything, just to remind yourself there's still a body here, still a you, still ground beneath you even when you can't feel it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's... actually small enough that I can almost imagine doing it, which surprises me because I expected something more complicated. But I'm a little skeptical, I guess — like, one breath and a hand on my chest, is that really going to do anything when I'm lying there thinking about how I'll never hear his voice again? I don't want to try it and have it feel completely hollow, because I think that might actually make things worse, like proof that nothing can touch this.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, pitched high, like there's both a flicker of hope and a real fear of having it extinguished — tells me this skepticism isn't resistance, it's actually you protecting something tender that's just starting to open up. You're right that one breath won't bring his voice back, and I'd never claim it will — what it does is interrupt that thirty-second spiral just enough so that the hour on the bed doesn't have to be inevitable every time, and that's not nothing, even if it's quiet. We could even try it right now together, not as proof it will fix anything, but just so the first time you meet it isn't alone at 7am when you're already underwater.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay... I'll try it, I guess, even though part of me feels a little self-conscious about it. I put my hand on my chest just now and took a breath, and it didn't feel hollow exactly, but it also didn't feel like much — just kind of neutral, which I suppose is better than nothing. I'm still not convinced it'll hold up against a 7am wave when I'm thinking about him specifically, but I can see how maybe it's worth having in my back pocket.
therapist: The fact that it landed as "neutral" rather than hollow is actually more significant than it might sound right now — neutral means the wave didn't win, and that's exactly what we're building toward, not transcendence, just a little bit of ground. I notice you're speaking quickly, like part of you is still bracing, still a little guarded about letting this matter too much — and that makes complete sense given how much has already been taken from you. But "worth having in my back pocket" is enough for today, and when 7am comes and you reach for it, you won't be trying it for the first time anymore — you'll already know what it feels like in your hand.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That last part actually got to me — "you won't be trying it for the first time anymore" — because I hadn't thought about it that way, like I've already done it once now and that counts for something. I'm still carrying a lot of doubt about whether any of this will really reach the parts that hurt most, the specific memories of him, his voice, the way he laughed. But I think I can at least try to remember that I've already held this once, even if it was just in a quiet therapy room and not at 7am when everything feels impossible.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but quick, with something almost fragile and bright underneath it — tells me that realization genuinely landed somewhere real, even as the doubt is still present alongside it, and I want you to hold both of those things without forcing one to cancel the other out. You're right that it counts — you have held it once, in a real moment of real pain, and that is a fact about you now that the 7am wave cannot take away. And those specific memories, his laugh, his voice — we don't have to protect you from those, we just have to make sure you have enough ground beneath you that you can let them move through you without losing yourself completely.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The idea that we don't have to protect me from his laugh or his voice — that actually feels different from what I expected, because I think I've been treating those memories like something dangerous, like if I let them in fully they'll just destroy me. But I'm not sure I know how to let something "move through" me rather than just flatten me — that sounds like a skill I definitely don't have yet. I guess I'm asking whether that's something we can actually work on, or whether it's one of those things that just happens on its own eventually, because I don't want to wait around hoping it gets easier without actually doing something.
therapist: The urgency in your voice right now — fast, loud, pitched high — tells me this question isn't abstract, it's almost like you're grabbing onto something and asking "can we actually do this, can we start now," and I want to meet that energy directly: yes, this is absolutely something we can work on together, it's not just a thing that happens passively while you wait. You've already named something really important — that you've been treating his laugh and his voice like threats to survive rather than parts of him to cherish — and that shift in how you relate to those memories is exactly the kind of thing CBT can help with, gently and deliberately. You don't have to have the skill yet; that's precisely why you're here, and we'll build it the same way we built today — one small, survivable moment at a time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: "Parts of him to cherish" — I hadn't framed it that way before, and hearing it said out loud made something shift a little, like maybe those memories aren't just landmines I have to tiptoe around. But I'm also aware that right now, in this room, it feels more possible than it's going to feel tomorrow morning when I'm alone and it hits without warning. I want to believe we can actually build this, I just don't want to leave here feeling hopeful and then have that hope collapse the second I'm back in my apartment without anyone around.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — soft but fast, pitched high, like something tender and frightened is trying to be heard — tells me that small shift you just felt is real, and so is the fear of losing it the moment you walk out the door, and both of those things deserve to be taken seriously. So let's make a small, concrete agreement before you leave today: tomorrow morning, if the wave comes, you put your hand on your chest, take one breath, and you say to yourself "these memories are parts of him to cherish" — not to make the pain disappear, but to meet it with something true instead of something terrifying. The hope doesn't have to hold up perfectly on its own, because you're not building it alone anymore — you're bringing it back here, and we keep building.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
